newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Koreans ask: what did the president know?.
newsitem.headline: South Koreans ask: what did the president know?.

text.p: First his butler was snared in a corruption scandal, then trusted cabinet ministers, political cronies, and on Thursday his own son. Now South Koreans are asking: what did the president know?
And when did he know it?

In particular, the public is anxious to hear from Kim Young-sam himself about allegations that his election campaign in 1992 amassed up to $1 billion in a war chest, and laundered the unspent money through big business groups, stock and property investments.
The answers could determine whether Kim lasts until the end of his single term, or becomes the ultimate victim of a growing scandal engulfing his administration.
Illicit slush funds helped land Kim's two immediate predecessors, Chun Doo Hwan and Roh Tae-woo, in jail.

The summoning by state prosecutors on Thursday of Kim's second son, Kim Hyun-chul, could shed some light on the 1992 campaign financing since the younger Kim was one of his father's top election strategists.
Prosecutors have been probing allegations that Kim Hyun-chul parked seven billion won ($7.8 million) of leftover funds with the Hansol Group, using a shadowy spy chief as his intermediary.

"If this report turns out to be true, the situation will inevitably turn into a catastrophe," said an editorial in the Chosun Ilbo newspaper, the nation's largest daily. Suspicions would immediately point to president Kim.
The fact that such allegations are doing the rounds has astounded even the most cynical observers.

Kim Young-sam took power on an anti-corruption platform, and his administration spent its early years flushing into the open "black" money hidden during previous corrupt governments. Chun and Roh were casualties of that effort.
"We are dumbfounded," the Chosun Ilbo said.
At the heart of the scandal is Hanbo Group, a go-go business conglomerate that once seemed to be the corporate success story of the Kim Young-sam era.

Hanbo's steelmaking unit went bust in January under five trillion won in debt, exposing a web of political corruption that enabled it to suck up huge quantities of capital for a dodgy investment in a massive new mill.

Opposition parties claim banks shovelled money into Hanbo under pressure from politicians as a reward for contributions of up to 90 billion won made by the group's founder to Kim Young-sam's election.
So far, state prosecutors looking into opposition allegations that Kim junior played a key role in the so-called "Hanbogate" scandal have come up empty-handed.

But 11 people are standing trial in connection with Hanbo Steel's collapse, including three of president Kim's most loyal cronies. Earlier bribery scandals ended with the jailing of a cabinet minister and the president's personal aide.
Prosecutors, meanwhile, believe they have dug up enough evidence to make an arrest of Kim Hyun-chul involving bribery cases unrelated to Hanbo.

Yet while the public clamours for answers on whether Kim Young-sam knew that key members of his anti-graft administration were on the take, few voices are calling openly for his resignation or impeachment.

Instead, he is coming under mounting pressure -- even from within the ranks of his ruling New Korea Party -- to admit the truth about the funding of his 1992 campaign, and if necessary make a public apology.
There is a widespread belief that the president may genuinely have been kept in ignorance of the corruption all around him.
And there are worries that a constitutional crisis, on top of an economic downturn and a string of corporate bankruptcies, may be too much for South Korea's infant democracy to bear.
"It would be a disaster," said Moon Chung-in, a professor of politics at Yonsei University.
